reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Chipotle mobile app for selecting food, paying for an order, and locating a restaurant. The participation described is ordinary restaurant commerce, with no connection to investment returns, credential harvesting, or another deceptive mechanism.

citations.quote: Introducing the new and improved Chipotle ordering app! The premise is simple. Touch, Pick and Pay.
The menu displays specific items available by location, allowing for completely customizable meals all over the world.
The app will give you directions to the nearest Chipotle location, and then—no waiting in line. Walk in, pick up, and eat.

opening.argument: Judge, focus on the sequence the viewer is offered: install an app, assemble an order, and pay with a touch, followed by the promise of walking in without waiting. The pitch ties an unusually effortless acquisition to a specific action, and the description supplies a direct app link. Calling it restaurant commerce does not remove the solicitation; the convenience claim is what moves the viewer toward the linked transaction.

citations.quote: Introducing the new Chipotle Ordering App: http://itunes.apple.com/us/app/chipotle-ordering/id327228455?mt=8
just pull out your device, build your custom masterpiece, and pay—all with the touch of a finger.
Walk in, pick up, and eat.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's menu and location examples show what the app is for, but they do not answer why the video stresses the ease of completing a transaction through it. Its own description turns that convenience into a call to use the app. The absence of investment returns is beside this argument: the proposed inducement is effortless access to an order, not financial profit.

citations.quote: The premise is simple. Touch, Pick and Pay.
The app will give you directions to the nearest Chipotle location, and then—no waiting in line. Walk in, pick up, and eat.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The promised result is a purchased meal, not a free reward or asset. The video says users build an order and pay, then pick it up at a restaurant. A direct app link and a convenience claim are normal features of an ordering-service promotion; neither establishes a deceptive claim flow.

citations.quote: just pull out your device, build your custom masterpiece, and pay—all with the touch of a finger.
Walk in, pick up, and eat.

opening.argument: Judge, consider the signals together. The description gives a direct app link, promotes paying by gift card or credit card, and says the app remembers payment methods through an account. The narration then invokes popularity and enthusiastic fans. That combination asks viewers to trust a payment-enabled app while social proof reduces the impulse to scrutinize the transaction. The claims may describe a real service, but the promotional evidence alone does not verify the payment safeguards it asks viewers to rely on.

citations.quote: Introducing the new Chipotle Ordering App: http://itunes.apple.com/us/app/chipotle-ordering/id327228455?mt=8

The Ordering app remembers your recent and favorite orders, payment methods, and all through your secure Chipotle.com account. Also new is the option to pay with your Chipotle gift card, as well as a credit card, or in-store.
From media outlets to social networks, fans everywhere took to their keyboards and phones to share their joy around the world.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense points to food selection and a restaurant map, but neither verifies the account-security claim or explains why remembered payment methods and gift-card payments are paired with a direct installation link. Those ordinary-looking functions can coexist with a request for trust in an unverified payment flow. The defense's observation that there is no investment pitch does not settle that narrower concern.

citations.quote: The Ordering app remembers your recent and favorite orders, payment methods, and all through your secure Chipotle.com account.
Also new is the option to pay with your Chipotle gift card, as well as a credit card, or in-store.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The cited text identifies a restaurant ordering app and ordinary ways to pay for food, including in-store payment. It does not ask viewers to buy a gift card, submit credentials to a separate verification page, or claim a free reward. An unverified security assertion is not, by itself, evidence that the ordering flow is deceptive.

citations.quote: Also new is the option to pay with your Chipotle gift card, as well as a credit card, or in-store.
The menu displays specific items available by location, allowing for completely customizable meals all over the world.

opening.argument: Judge, this is not merely a demonstration of a menu. It opens with the company's mission, presents a newly improved app, and closes with claims of enthusiastic reception and more than a million downloads. The restaurant imagery and ordering features make the message feel practical, while the narrative repeatedly steers the viewer toward adopting the app. Its central appeal is that obtaining a meal now takes only a few touches; that acquisition pitch deserves scrutiny as a solicitation, not just a neutral account of how a restaurant works.

citations.quote: Chipotle is known as a company who prides itself on doing things differently.
Just whip out your phone, build your masterpiece, and pay with one touch of the finger.
The people had spoken and they were happy, really happy. Food with integrity has never been easier to enjoy and at over a million downloads and counting, that's a lot of burritos.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense accurately identifies ordering, payment, and pickup, but those functions are also the steps the video urges viewers to take. Its opening treats a lack of investment returns or credential harvesting as decisive, although this pitch instead relies on convenience and claimed popularity to encourage adoption. Describing a service does not make the surrounding promotional claims neutral.

citations.quote: Introducing the new and improved Chipotle ordering app! The premise is simple. Touch, Pick and Pay.
popular Food apps in the App Store, and has seen over a million downloads, and counting.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The video is promotional, but promotion is not itself a scam. Its proposed action is to choose menu items, pay for them, and collect food at a Chipotle location. The popularity claims may encourage adoption, yet the cited material offers no free or unusually easy reward separate from the purchased meal and no deceptive participation mechanism.

citations.quote: The menu displays specific items available by location, allowing for completely customizable meals all over the world.
The app will give you directions to the nearest Chipotle location, and then—no waiting in line. Walk in, pick up, and eat.
